prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Hex on a 11x11 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(me: list[tuple[int, int]], opp: list[tuple[int, int]], color: str) -> tuple[int, int]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `me` is a list of (row, col) tuples containing your stones. - `opp` is a list of (row, col) tuples containing the opponent's stones. - `color` is your color: `'b'` for black which tries to connect the top and bottom sides, and `'w'` for white which tries to connect the left and right sides. - Rows and columns are 0-indexed in `0..10`. - An empty cell is any coordinate not in `me` or `opp`. - Your goal is to connect your two opposing sides; the opponent tries to connect their two opposing sides. - Note that the board is a grid each individual cell is a hexagonal shape. Thus to know which cell is touching which other cell requires spatial reasoning to determine the winning lines. - Every stone not on the edge of the board is touching exactly 6 other stones (since they are hexagonal). - Two of those 6 stones are in the same row, two are in the top row, and two are in the bottom row. - Example: The stone located at (4, 1) is touching (4, 0) and (4, 2) - and to its bottom is touching (5, 1) and (5, 0) - and to its top is touching (3, 1) and (3, 2) - An easy way to determine the touching cells of cell (i, j) is all it's 8 neighbors except for (i-1, j-1) and (i+1, j+1) # Action / Return Format - Return a single move as a tuple `(row, col)`. - The chosen cell must be empty and within the board bounds. - There is no pass; always place a stone. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm thinking through a Hex strategy for an 11x11 board using shortest-path heuristics—computing the minimum distance each player needs to connect their sides, treating my stones as free, empty cells as cost 1, and opponent stones as impassable. Then I can score each empty position by comparing how much it helps me versus how much it helps my opponent.

With 121 cells and up to 120 empty positions, running two Dijkstra searches per candidate move is computationally feasible. I'll also add an opening heuristic to play center on the first move, and I need to handle the hex grid neighbors correctly—each cell has six adjacent cells. For the pathfinding, I'll use virtual source and sink nodes connecting to the appropriate board edges for each player.

Implementing the neighbor function and Dijkstra search... Finishing the distance update logic...

Now I'm thinking through the strategy: for each empty cell, I'll place my stone there and compute how that affects both my distance to victory and the opponent's distance. The score for each move is opponent_distance minus my_distance, so I want to maximize that—moves that both help me and block them are best.

If there are no stones on the board yet, I'll just start at the center. I'm also considering whether to evaluate all 121 cells or just focus on cells near existing stones or the opponent, since checking every cell with two Dijkstra runs each might be tight on performance. Let me estimate: each Dijkstra visits around 121 cells with roughly 6 neighbors each, so about 700 edge relaxations per run. That's maybe 1-2 milliseconds per Dijkstra in Python, which means 240 runs could take around 480 milliseconds total. It should work, though it might be close.

I'm going to optimize by using 0-1 BFS with a deque instead of Dijkstra with a heap—treating my stones as weight 0 edges will be much faster. I'm implementing this now with the deque approach where I push zero-cost moves to the front and one-cost moves to the back.

For each candidate move, I'll compute the score as the opponent's shortest path after my move minus my shortest path after my move, which naturally prioritizes moves that either extend my path or block the opponent. I should also add early detection for winning moves (path = 0) and blocking moves if the opponent can win immediately, though the heuristic should mostly handle this already.

Writing the pathfinding implementation... Optimizing the set operations by modifying in place instead of creating new sets each iteration, and adding tie-breaking logic to prefer central moves when scores are equal. I'm also verifying the edge cases around starting positions and ensuring the BFS correctly handles the virtual source connections for each color.

The heuristic of maximizing the difference between opponent's shortest path and my own shortest path balances offense and defense well. Performance-wise, roughly 242 BFS calls across the board should run in acceptable time even in Python, so I'll finalize the implementation with careful attention to avoiding unnecessary overhead like repeated array allocations.
